Grok: “The Byrd Rule’s this batshit, 1980s-era Senate filter that makes sure budget reconciliation bills don’t turn into a free-for-all where senators sneak in whatever pet project they’re obsessed with. Named after Senator Robert Byrd, it’s like the ultimate buzzkill for anything that doesn’t scream “money” in a straight line. It says provisions in a reconciliation bill—used to fast-track budget stuff with a simple majority—have to directly mess with federal spending or revenue. No fluff, no side quests. If it’s more about policy, like who gets Medicaid or whether kittens get free hugs, it’s out, even if it saves a buck. The parliamentarian, like Elizabeth MacDonough, gets to play grim reaper, slashing anything that smells too “policy-ish.” It’s why Tuberville’s anti-immigrant Medicaid ban got yeeted—it’s not about dollars, it’s about who’s in or out. The rule’s got six tests, but the big one’s this: if the budget impact’s just “incidental” to the policy goal, it’s dead. Imagine trying to convince a robot accountant your vibe affects GDP—it’s that level of fuckery.”
